evidence: This case is about the cancellation of “Draggieland,” an annual student-funded drag show at Texas A&M, due to a drag ban implemented by the university’s Board of Regents (“Board”).

On March 5, 2025, the student organization that produces Draggieland, Texas A&M Queer Empowerment Council (“Council”), filed suit against Texas A&M in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas.
The Council sued under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, alleging that the university’s prohibition of drag violated the students’ right to free speech.
The Council also argued that the Board violated the Texas Open Meetings Act by holding a meeting without providing proper notice.
According to the Council, because the drag ban was promulgated at this illegally-held meeting, it was void.

Represented by the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, the Council sought: (1) a temporary restraining order to prevent the cancellation of Draggieland, (2) an injunction against the enforcement of the Board’s drag ban, (3) an injunction to void any action taken by the Board at the meeting where it established the drag ban, and (4) declaratory relief.
The District Court ruled in favor of the Council on March 24, 2025, enjoining Texas A&M from enforcing the drag ban and permitting Draggieland to proceed as scheduled.
On March 28, 2025, Texas A&M filed an appeal and requested a stay of the preliminary injunction. As of March 31, 2025, this case was ongoing.
The case was assigned to District Judge Lee Hyman Rosenthal.

evidence: This case challenged the freezing of federal grant funds meant for community financial development.
Plaintiffs, Inclusiv, Inc., a nonprofit financial institution, filed a lawsuit in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia.
The plaintiffs named Citibank, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), and the EPA Administrator as defendants.
Inclusiv sought injunctive relief and damages, claiming the defendants unlawfully blocked access to grant funds that had already been awarded and disbursed.
The dispute stemmed from the National Clean Investment Fund (NCIF), a program under the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund (GGRF), which Congress established through the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022.

Inclusiv was selected as a grantee in April 2024 and awarded $1.87 billion under the CCIA grant program, allowing them to make commitments to 108 credit unions to help low and moderate-income communities reduce energy costs, create jobs, and improve financial security.
Under the terms of the grant, the funds were held at Citibank, which served as a financial agent under an Account Control Agreement (ACA) executed with the EPA.
The dispute arose in February 2025, when the EPA allegedly froze Inclusiv’s GGRF funds, preventing the organization from distributing them to community lenders.
This came following the EPA Administrator’s public remarks expressing his opposition to the GGRF, calling it “criminal” and vowing to recover the funds.
On March 11, 2025, the EPA formally terminated Inclusiv’s grant, citing unspecified compliance concerns.
Simultaneously, Citibank, which managed Inclusiv’s grant funds under an Account Control Agreement (ACA), declined to process any disbursements.

On March 18, 2025, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia issued a TRO in Climate United Fund v. Citibank [../../../../case/46274/], halting the effects of the March 11 termination letter.
In reliance on the TRO order, Inclusiv sought disbursement of funds on March 21.
Citibank did not respond to this letter, nor disperse any funds.
On March 31, Inclusive filed its complaint alleging claims against both the EPA and Citibank.

Against the EPA, it claimed the agency’s actions violated the Administrative Procedure Act for engaging in actions that were contrary to federal law and EPA regulations, and for being arbitrary and capricious.
It also claimed that the EPA violated the Separation of Powers and the Vesting, Spending and Appropriations, and Take Care Clauses by failing to distribute funds appropriated by Congress.
Additionally, Inclusiv claimed the EPA deprived it of the Fifth Amendment right to Due Process by terminating its funds without notice or an opportunity to be heard.

Finally, plaintiffs asserted an Ultra Vires claim that the EPA exceeded their constitutional and statutory authority under the “Administrative Procedure Act, the Inflation Reduction Act, the Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act, and the Anti-Deficiency Act by withholding obligated funds in contravention of these plain congressional mandates.”
Against Citibank, plaintiffs asserted state law claims of breach of contract and conversion.

Plaintiffs sought a declaration that (1) the notice of termination was void; (2) the suspension of the grant award violated the APA, Separation of Powers, and the Due Process Clause, and exceeded statutory authority conferred on the EPA; (3) and that Citibank’s freezing of Inclusiv’s account was contrary to law and violated their contractual obligations under the ACA.

They also requested a permanent injunction prohibiting the enforcement of the March 11 termination letter, and enjoining defendants from "[s]uspending, terminating, or attempting to suspend or terminate Inclusiv’s grant award, except as permitted by governing law."
On April 1, plaintiffs filed both a preliminary injunction motion and a temporary restraining order (TRO).

The preliminary injunction motion requested the Court to prevent the government defendants from enforcing the March 11 termination letter or suspending Inclusiv’s grant award, and Citibank from violating its contractual obligations under the ACA.
The TRO requested a restoration of the plaintiffs’ grant funds to its Citibank account, which had been removed when Inclusiv’s CFO checked the balance of its Citibank account on April 1.

Plaintiffs previously did not seek a TRO on reliance on the EPA’s statement that they would not move the money while the TRO in Climate United Fund v. Citibank [../../../../case/46274/] was in effect.
There was a dispute over the nature of this removal, as defendants argued this was a routine transfer that occurred monthly.
Plaintiffs stated that if the money was returned to their account, they would withdraw their request for TRO.
However, they requested that the Court engage in more careful monitoring of the money.
On April 1, plaintiffs also filed notice of a related case, Climate United Fund v. Citibank.
The court consolidated this case with Climate United Fund v. Citibank on April 15.

On April 16, in light of the preliminary injunction granted in Climate United Fund v. Citibank and this case's consolidation with Climate United Fund, the Court denied the plaintiffs' motion for preliminary injunction as moot.
Further updates on this case can be found on Climate United Fund's Clearinghouse page [../../../../case/46274/].

evidence: This case is one of numerous lawsuits challenging the Trump administration’s abrupt termination of immigration visas—mostly student or work visas—with no notice to the visa-holders and with dubious or no legal basis.

On April 11, 2025, five international students—attending school on F-1 visas—filed this lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, against President Donald Trump, the Secretary of Homeland Security, the Acting Director of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and the Acting Director of the ICE San Francisco Field Office.

In early April, the defendants had abruptly terminated the plaintiffs', and other international students’, record in the Student and Exchange Visitor Information (SEVIS) system, effectively stripping them of their ability to remain a student in the United States.

The plaintiffs alleged that the defendants actions were unlawful and designed to coerce them and other international students into abandoning their studies and self-deporting in contravention to the Administrative Procedure Act and the Fifth Amendment.
The plaintiffs argue that SEVIS termination is unlawful unless a student actually violates the terms of their status, and they argue that none of them did.
They seek declaratory and injunctive relief restoring their SEVIS status and preventing further enforcement actions or removal based on the unlawful terminations.

On April 16, the plaintiffs moved for a temporary restraining order (TRO) to enjoin the defendants from (1) arresting and incarcerating the plaintiffs pending the resolution of these proceedings; (2) transferring the plaintiffs outside the jurisdiction of this district pending the resolution of these proceedings; and (3) preventing any legal effect that the unlawful termination of the plaintiffs' SEVIS statuses or the potential unlawful revocation of their F-1 visas may have.
The following day, the court granted the plaintiffs' motion for a TRO, preserving the status quo pending further developments in this case.
The case was then marked as related to Doe v. Trump, 4:25-cv-03140  and reassigned to that case's judge, Jeffrey White, who held a hearing on April 25 and extended the TRO.

The case was later marked related to Doe v. Trump, reassigned to Judge Jeffrey White, who held a hearing on April 25 and extended the TRO. This case is part of a broader litigation challenging the Trump administration’s abrupt termination of immigration visas, which typically lacked notice and legal basis.

evidence: On April 7, 2025, a coal miner filed this lawsuit in the United States District Court for the Southern District of West Virginia against the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and its Secretary.
Represented by private counsel, the Plaintiff challenged the termination of HHS employees overseeing the screening and job transfer programs related to coal mine dust lung disease (CMDLD).

The Plaintiff, seeking to represent a class of similarly situated coal miners, argued that the termination of these HHS employees endangered him and other coal miners and violated the Administrative Procedure Act.
The court held an evidentiary hearing on May 7 and on May 13 issued a preliminary injunction.

The court found that the plaintiff had standing, since as "an active coal miner with diagnosed black lung, he is within the group intended to be protected by the Mine Act and Part 90, and he is among those served by the CWHSP at NIOSH," and is therefore harmed by the elimination of those services.

The court found that through the elimination of the vast majority of employees at the Respiratory Health Division (RHD) and the CWSHP, the agencies had been shut down, constituting final agency action reviewable under the APA.
The court then found the defendants' actions to be arbitrary and capricious and contrary to law under the APA.

Under the Mine Act and associated regulations, HHS is required to "to provide medical examinations to screen for black lung, to evaluate chest radiographs and spirometry tests, to issue Part 90 findings to miners with signs of black lung, to maintain a mobile health unit that travels to mines and mining communities, to maintain the B-Reader program, and to provide chest autopsies to examine for black lung in deceased miners."
However, with the terminations of the employees, HHS was not fulfilling those obligations.
The injunction requires restoration of all personnel and continuation of the miner health programs at issue.
The court also ordered that, in the event of a reorganization at HHS, there be no pause in the protections mandated by statute.
extracted.value: The case involves a coal miner filing a lawsuit on April 7, 2025, against the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) for terminating employees responsible for coal mine dust lung disease (CMDLD) screening and job transfer programs, arguing that these terminations endangered miners and violated the Administrative Procedure Act; the court found the plaintiff standing, that the terminations shut down agencies and were arbitrary and capricious, and ordered restoration of personnel and continuation of miner health programs, with background obligations under the Mine Act and Part 90 requiring HHS to provide medical examinations, evaluations, findings, mobile units, B-Reader program, and autopsies.

evidence: This case is one of several lawsuits challenging the Trump administration’s use of the Alien Enemies Act to detain and deport noncitizens without due process.
On May 17, 2025, a Venezuelan noncitizen detained in the Central District of California brought this habeas and civil lawsuit as a proposed class action.

The petition-complaint names President Donald Trump, the Attorney General, the U.S. Department of Defense and its Secretary, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and its Secretary, the U.S. Department of State and its Secretary, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and its Acting Director and LA Director, and other ICE officials as Defendants.
The case challenged both ICE's notice practices for noncitizens facing removal under the Alien Enemies Act, and the underlying question of the legitimate application of the Act.

On May 19, 2025, Judge Holcomb issued a class wide preliminary injunction - issued ex parte - prohibiting the government from removing any putative class members from the Central District of California pursuant to the Alien Enemies Act, pending a hearing on a motion for preliminary injunction.
On June 2, Judge Holcomb rejected government arguments challenging jurisdiction and standing, extended the preliminary injunction, and certified the class.

Judge Holcomb found that petitioner was unlikely to succeed on his challenge to the Alien Enemies Act because the act granted "close to unlimited" power to the President to determine the applicability of the act.

In contrast, Judge Holcomb found the petitioner likely to succeed in establishing a violation of his due process rights particularly because the government declined to provide necessary details about the process they proposed to employ.

On June 20, Judge Holcomb denied petitioner's ex party application for a permanent injunction without prejudice and ordered the government "to file a Status Report no later than July 10, 2025, and every 30 days thereafter, that advises the Court regarding the status of the Government's appeal in [petitioner's] removal and asylum proceedings."
The case is ongoing.

Regarding the Preferred Names Policy, the court found that the policy was neutral (i.e. did not target plaintiffs’ religion) and that the policy rationally related to defendant’s legitimate goal of complying with Title IX and avoiding discrimination against transgender students. Therefore, the court denied preliminary injunction relating to the Preferred Names Policy and allowed the policy to remain in effect while the case proceeded. Regarding the Student Privacy Policy, the court similarly found plaintiffs’ first amendment claim unpersuasive, since the policy was neutral and did not target plaintiffs’ religion. Furthermore, the court was largely unpersuaded by plaintiffs’ due process claims to direct the upbringing of their child and to familial privacy, reasoning that plaintiffs were asking the court to extend both due process rights far beyond the bounds of current case law. On the other hand, the court took issue with the portion of the Student Privacy Policy which required school staff to keep a student’s preferred name and pronouns secret from parents even if a parent asks, including lying to parents if necessary. The court found that such a policy “shocks the conscience” and could cause irreparable harm to plaintiffs. Under this reasoning, the court partially granted preliminary injunction. Specifically, absent a reasonable concern of physical harm or abuse, the court enjoined the school district from precluding a school district employee from responding to a parent’s inquiry regarding their child’s requested name or pronouns or requiring an employee to lie to parents about a student’s requested name or pronouns. In all other respects, the court denied plaintiffs’ motion for preliminary injunction. 680 F.Supp.3d 1250.

evidence: In October 2017, the Special Litigation Section of the Civil Rights Division at the U.S. Department of Justice and the United States Attorney’s Office for the District of South Carolina (collectively, “the DOJ”) initiated an investigation of the South Carolina Department of Juvenile Justice (SCDJJ) pursuant to the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), the Civil Rights of Institutionalized Persons Act (CRIPA), and the Violent Crime and Law Enforcement Act.
The investigation was focused on the Broad River Road Complex (BRRC), which was South Carolina’s long-term juvenile commitment facility.
To complete its investigation, the DOJ conducted several onsite tours and interviews, and reviewed available video footage of instances related to the alleged violations.

The DOJ continued its investigation and issued a second findings report on April 14, 2022, concluding that: 1) the conditions at the BRRC violated the due process clause of the Fourteenth Amendment and 2) the violations were pursuant to a pattern or practice of resistance to the full enjoyment of rights protected by the Fourteenth Amendment.

In addition to issuing its findings, the DOJ made several suggestions for remedial measures: • improve the physical plan to ensure adequate surveillance and retain video to enable facility leadership to investigate allegations of abuse;   • conduct a staffing study to determine the appropriate staffing levels and staffing patterns to adequately supervise youth in the male living units, and make changes to staffing patterns as necessary;   • train staff on positive behavior management tools and de-escalation to reduce youth-on-youth violence and the use of isolation as a response to youth behavior;   • eliminate the use of isolation for minor misbehavior, protective custody, and mental health observation;   • replace long-term isolation with a short-term cool-down room in each housing unit for youth who are a threat to safety and develop policies to ensure that youth who are placed in the cool-down room are returned to the general population as soon as they are no longer a threat to safety;   • develop admissions screening protocols to identify youth who are vulnerable to victimization by other youth in the facility and create a specialized housing unit for these youth with access to equal recreational and educational services as youth in the general population;   • develop agreements with the state Department of Mental Health to ensure the prompt transfer of suicidal youth to appropriate placements for mental health treatment;   • revise the use of force policy to emphasize age-appropriate interactions and de-escalation techniques, make clear that force may be used only to prevent imminent potential harm to staff or others, require timely reporting and review of all uses of force, and require immediate training and corrective action where staff action does not conform to the policy;   • train staff on age-appropriate interactions with young people and adolescent development, de-escalation techniques, positive behavior management responses, and the revised use of force policy; and   • conduct timely investigations of allegations of staff-on-youth harms, including retention of all relevant video footage, and at the conclusion of each investigation, conduct necessary training to prevent future harms and impose discipline, as appropriate, for abuses of young people.

Also on April 14, 2022, the DOJ filed a complaint pursuant to the Violent Crime and Law Enforcement Act. On the same day, the DOJ filed a settlement agreement resolving its investigation in the U.S. District Court for the District of South Carolina. The matter was assigned to Judge Mary Geiger Lewis. In the agreement, the SCDJJ agreed to implement all of the DOJ's suggested remedial measures. The agreement also appointed an independent subject matter expert to monitor the agreement and make recommendations to ensure the SCDJJ’s compliance. Lastly, the agreement would expire in 5 years so long as SCDJJ attained substantial compliance with all provisions and maintained that compliance for one year. The parties jointly moved to conditionally dismiss the case and requested that the court retain jurisdiction to enforce the settlement agreement permitting reinstatement of the action in case of breach.

evidence: CMS, which is a subagency of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), proposed the challenged rule in March 2025, soon after the Trump Administration took office. The rule, entitled 'Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; Marketplace Integrity and Affordability,' allegedly added several roadblocks to the acquisition of ACA health insurance; these included new fees, reductions in the enrollment period, and even a revocation of the ACA's central promise that any American can purchase health insurance.

Plaintiffs the City of Columbus, the Mayor and City Council of Baltimore, the City of Chicago, Doctors for America, and the Main Street Alliance filed this lawsuit on July 1, 2025, in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland. The lawsuit named HHS, its Secretary, CMS, and its Administrator as defendants. Plaintiffs were represented by Democracy Forward. Plaintiffs sought a declaration that the CMS rule was unlawful under the APA; vacatur of the rule; a stay of, and preliminary and permanent injunctions against, the rule's enforcement; and attorneys' fees. The case was assigned to Judge Brendan Abell Hurson.

On July 2, 2025, plaintiffs filed a motion requesting a stay, or alternatively a preliminary injunction, of the new CMS rule. The municipal plaintiffs argued that as healthcare providers of last resort for those who lose insurance under the new rule, the rule would bestow a heavy financial burden on them. The organizational plaintiffs argued that the rule would make it harder for them to pay their employees or to receive adequate compensation for healthcare services rendered.

The court held a hearing on the requested preliminary injunction on August 14, 2025. On August 22, 2025, it issued an order granting in part and denying in part the plaintiffs' motion and entering a stay enjoining certain provisions of the CMS rule that were to take effect on August 25. 2025 WL 2426382. It reasoned that the plaintiffs had shown a likelihood of success on the merits of their challenges to seven provisions of the rule, but that they failed to show likelihood of success on the merits sufficient to warrant preliminary relief as to their remaining challenges to two other provisions of the rule.

First, the court found that Main Street Alliance and the city plaintiffs had standing based on the increased premiums and uncompensated care costs that would be 'predictable results' of the challenged provisions.

As to the first category, the court held that CMS lacked authority to impose the challenged fees, which were untethered to the statutory formula, and that plaintiffs were likely to succeed on their claim that the agency acted in an arbitrary and capricious manner by revising the actuarial value policy because it provided an insufficient and conclusory rationale for the changes.

As to the second category, the court held that plaintiffs were likely to succeed on their challenge to past-due payment requirements, because the agency was not authorized to create a new exception to the ACA’s categorical guaranteed-issue rule, and to the verification requirements provision because defendants’ rationale for imposing the requirements was not indicative of reasoned decision-making.

Next, the court first held that plain text of the ACA contradicted the agency’s failure-to-reconcile provision, and therefore that plaintiffs were likely to succeed on their claim that the provision was imposed contrary to law.

Ultimately, the court held that the appropriate course of action was to temporarily stay the seven challenged provisions as to which it found likelihood of success on the merits, postponing the effective date until final resolution of the lawsuit.  It reasoned that the U.S. Supreme Court’s recent decision in  CASA  [../../../../case/45965/] did not preclude such relief, because that decision did not limit a court’s ability to preliminarily set aside new agency rules under the APA.
This case is ongoing.
extracted.value: The case involves a lawsuit filed on July 1, 2025 by the City of Columbus, the Mayor and City Council of Baltimore, the City of Chicago, Doctors for America, and the Main Street Alliance against the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, its Secretary, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, and its Administrator, challenging a CMS rule proposed in March 2025 entitled 'Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; Marketplace Integrity and Affordability' that allegedly added new fees, reduced enrollment periods, and revoked the ACA's guarantee that any American can purchase insurance. Plaintiffs sought a declaration that the rule was unlawful under the APA, vacatur, a stay, and injunctions. On August 22, 2025, Judge Brendan Abell Hurson granted a stay of seven provisions effective August 25, 2025, based on plaintiffs' likelihood of success and irreparable harm, while denying relief for two provisions. The stayed provisions include a $5 premium penalty on automatic re-enrollees, revocation of guaranteed coverage for past‑due premiums, failure to reconcile policy, eligibility verification for the special enrollment period, verification of income inconsistencies, changes to de minimis ranges for actuarial value calculations, and changes to self‑attestation of projected income. The provisions not stayed are the change to the premium adjustment percentage and the elimination of the 60‑day extension for resolving income inconsistencies. The court found standing based on increased premiums and uncompensated care costs, and held that CMS lacked authority to impose certain fees and acted arbitrarily on others. The court reasoned that the Supreme Court’s recent decision in CASA did not preclude such relief. The case is ongoing.

evidence: On April 10, 2025, sixteen states and the District of Columbia filed this lawsuit in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York against the U.S. Department of Education and its Secretary.
The states challenged Defendants' revocation of the state's access to funds appropriated to help public schools recover from the effects of COVID-19.
They alleged that Defendants' actions violated the Administrative Procedure Act.
On April 11, Plaintiffs moved for a preliminary injunction, subject to an expedited briefing schedule agreed with the Defendants and ordered by the court on April 15.
On May 6, the court held argument and the same day issued a preliminary injunction.

The injunction blocked the challenged reaction letters and further prohibited Defendants from taking any action to modify previously-granted grant approvals without 14 days' notice to the affected state.
On June 4, the court extended the preliminary injunction.
That same day, Defendants filed a notice of appeal to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit.
On June 6, in the Court of Appeals, they moved for a stay pending appeal and requested an immediate administrative stay while the motion was under consideration.
On June 10, the court referred the stay motion to the three-judge motions panel scheduled for June 17 and denied the request for an administrative stay in light of the expedited briefing schedule.
On June 20, the Court of Appeals denied Defendant-Appellants' motion to stay the district court's order.

The Court found that the record supported the conclusion that the Government's actions were likely arbitrary and capricious, and that they failed to meaningfully consider the reliance interests at stake.
The Court further determined that a stay would substantially injure the plaintiff states.
The case is ongoing.

evidence: Issued on May 1, 2025, Executive Order 14290, “Ending Taxpayer Subsidization of Biased Media,” required federal agencies to withhold all funding from National Public Radio (NPR) and the Public Broadcasting Service (PBS) and barred local stations receiving federal grants from using those funds to purchase their programming.
On May 27, 2025, NPR, Colorado Public Radio, Aspen Public Radio, and KSUT Public Radio filed this lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia.

The plaintiffs sued President Donald Trump and several federal agencies and officials, including the Office of Management and Budget, the U.S. Department of the Treasury, the National Endowment for the Arts, and the Corporation for Public Broadcasting.
The plaintiffs sued under the First and Fifth Amendments, and the Administrative Procedure Act.

On May 30, 2025, PBS filed a parallel suit [../../../../case/46646/] against President Trump and federal agencies, challenging Executive Order 14290 as an unlawful effort to defund public media for political reasons.
On June 10, 2025, the court granted a joint proposal from the parties to resolve the case through cross-motions for summary judgment.

On June 13, 2025, the plaintiffs filed their motion for summary judgment, asserting that the Executive Order lacked any legal basis and violated the APA, the First Amendment, Fifth Amendment, the Spending Clause, and the Public Broadcasting Act’s mandate of editorial independence.
On July 12, 2025, the defendants moved for summary judgment and opposed the plaintiffs’ motion, arguing the case was unripe because no funding had been terminated and no concrete injury suffered.
On July 25, 2025, the plaintiffs opposed the defendants’ cross-motion and replied in support of their own, arguing the Executive Order was “textbook retaliation and viewpoint discrimination.”
The plaintiffs argued the order exceeded presidential authority and constituted retaliation, viewpoint discrimination, and infringement of associational rights.
The defendants argued no Fifth Amendment violation because federal grants are not protected property interests.
The defendants argued the President is not subject to the APA and that no agency had taken final action subject to statutory challenge.
This case is about whether the President of the United States can unilaterally strip public broadcasters of federal funding based on perceived political bias.

PBS filed a parallel suit on May 30, 2025. The plaintiffs sought a declaration that the order was unlawful and an injunction preventing agencies from cutting funds to NPR, PBS, or their affiliates, citing retaliation, viewpoint discrimination, and infringement of associational rights. The defendants moved for summary judgment on July 12, 2025, arguing the case was unripe and that the order did not violate constitutional or statutory provisions. The plaintiffs opposed the defendants’ motion on July 25, 2025, asserting the order was retaliation and viewpoint discrimination, was unconstitutionally vague, and deprived NPR of a protected property interest in federal funding. evidence: In 2022, the Southern Education Foundation (SEF) was awarded a five-year, discretionary grant by the Department of Education (ED) to operate the Equity Assistance Center-South (EAC-South).
This grant was terminated abruptly by President Trump’s Executive Order 14173, which directed the ED to terminate funding for programs that promote or take part in DEI initiatives.

On April 9, 2025, represented by private counsel, the Southern Education Foundation filed this lawsuit against President Donald Trump, the ED, and the Secretary of Education in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia.

The SEF brought three separate claims under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA): that the grant termination was arbitrary and capricious, that the termination failed to comply with relevant rules, and that it failed to comport with Due Process Procedures.

The SEF also brought a Fifth Amendment claim, a First Amendment claim and a claim under VI of the Civil Rights Act. Lastly, the SEF brought an ultra vires claim, alleging that the grant termination exceeded the scope of the DOE’s authority.

The SEF requested that the court enjoin the Defendants from terminating SEF’s EAC-South grant award, from taking adverse action based on the original notice of grant termination, and from withholding any funds owed to SEF under the grant.
Judge Friedman granted the SEF's motion for a preliminary injunction on May 21, 2025.
Southern Education Foundation v. United States Dep. of Ed., F. Supp. 3d., 2025 WL 1453047 (D.D.C 2025).
The government appealed the preliminary injunction.

evidence: This case challenged the termination of a $6 million award under the Bipartisan Safer Communities Act to the Board of Education for the Silver Consolidated Schools (Board).

On February 14, 2025, the Department of Education (DOE), by and through its Acting Assistant Secretary for Civil Rights, issued a Dear Colleague Letter (DCL) threatening schools and colleges across the country with the loss of federal funding if these education institutions continued to pursue ambiguously defined 'DEI programs' that 'teach students that certain racial groups bear unique moral burdens that others do not' and/or 'stigmatize students who belong to racial groups.'

The Department of Education canceled the grants to the Board on April 29, 2025, announcing that the grants 'violate the letter or purpose of Federal civil rights law; conflict with the Department’s policy of prioritizing merit, fairness, and excellence in education; undermine the well-being of the students these programs are intended to help; or constitute an inappropriate use of federal funds.'
The Board sued on June 20, 2025, in the District Court for the District of New Mexico.
The Board alleged that the termination of the grants violated the First Amendment's Free Speech Clause, violated the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause, and violated the Spending Clause.
The Board also claimed that the termination was void for vagueness, was ultra vires, and was contrary to law and arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act.
The Board asked the court to declare the DOE's actions unlawful and to enjoin the DOE from terminating the Board's grants.
Judge Johnson denied the plaintiffs' motion on July 21 and dismissed the case without prejudice.

"The non-continuation of Plaintiff’s grant funding is the type of contract claim that gives rise to Tucker Act jurisdiction." "Rather than challenging a regulatory action with some monetary implications, Plaintiff seeks payment of 'the grant monies' it claims entitlement to," which is the essence of a contract claim.

The court also rejected the plaintiffs' Spending Clause claim, since under the statutory framework, the Secretary is required to determine whether the continuation of the grant is in the 'best interests of the Federal Government.' The Secretary made that determination here, and the decision to terminate the plaintiffs' grant was within that discretion.
This discretion also doomed the plaintiffs' ultra vires claim, since the defendants did not act outside of their authority.

Finally, on the plaintiffs' APA claims, the court held that the defendants' decision on how to allocate a grant award 'seems like a quintessential decision committed to agency discretion by law,' meaning that it would not be reviewable under the APA.
Based on these findings, the court said that the plaintiffs could not succeed on their request for preliminary injunction, given that they were unlikely to succeed on the merits of their claims.
Therefore, the court rejected the plaintiffs' request and, based on its holding that the claims were contractual in nature, dismissed the case for lack of jurisdiction.
The case is ongoing.

evidence: On April 4, 2025, the Association for Education Finance and Policy, Inc. and the Institute for Higher Education Policy filed a lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia.
They argued that the Department was acting illegally by shutting down the Institute of Education Sciences (IES), an agency created by Congress.

These actions included the mass cancellation of contracts that supported IES research, the elimination of approximately 90% of IES staff positions, and the termination of remote access for outside researchers to existing data.

The plaintiffs asked the court to declare the defendants' actions unlawful and to issue several orders. These included orders to restore the terminated contracts, vacate the reduction in force of IES employees, and reverse the termination of remote access to restricted-use data.

They also requested the court to prevent the defendants from taking any further actions that would hinder IES's ability to perform its legally required tasks and sought a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction to immediately stop the shutdown of IES.

According to the lawsuit, Congress established IES in 2002 to conduct and share high-quality research, statistics, and evaluations related to education from early childhood through postsecondary study.

• The plaintiffs asserted a non‑statutory claim arguing that the defendants' actions were ultra vires, meaning they went beyond their legal powers and encroached upon the authority of Congress, which created IES.   • They claimed that the defendants violated the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) by acting contrary to law, specifically the Education Sciences Reform Act of 2002 and the Higher Education Opportunity Act, which established IES and its responsibilities.   • The plaintiffs argued that the defendants' actions were arbitrary and capricious under the APA because they offered no reasoned explanation and failed to consider the impact on researchers and other stakeholders who rely on IES.   • They claimed a violation of the APA based on the Impoundment Control Act, alleging that the defendants unlawfully rescinded or deferred funds appropriated by Congress for IES.   • Lastly, the plaintiffs asserted a violation of the APA based on the Anti‑Deficiency Act, arguing that the defendants illegally refused to spend funds Congress had allocated to IES.
On June 3, Judge McFadden denied the plaintiffs' motion for a preliminary injunction.

On June 18, the plaintiffs filed an amended complaint challenging the termination of eight specific programs run by the Department of Education: (1) the termination of the National Postsecondary Student Aid Study;  (2) the termination of the 2020/25 Beginning Postsecondary Students Longitudinal Study; (3) the termination of the High School Longitudinal Study of 2009; (4) the termination of the High School and Beyond Longitudinal Study of 2022; (5) the termination of the Early Childhood Longitudinal Study-Kindergarten: 2024; (6) the termination of IES’s peer review program for new grant funding; (7) the termination of IES’s program for remote access to restricted‑use data; and (8) the termination of processing applications for access to restricted‑use data.

On July 2, the defendants filed a motion to dismiss, arguing that the court still lacked jurisdiction over the plaintiffs' claims under the Tucker Act, and that the plaintiffs still were making a programmatic challenge, rather than a challenge to a discrete, final agency action as required by the APA.

On July 16, the plaintiffs filed a second amended complaint removing the challenges to two of the terminations mentioned in the first amended complaint: the National Postsecondary Student Aid Study and IES's program for remote access to restricted‑use data.
Given the second amended complaint, the court denied as moot the defendants' motion to dismiss and ordered them to file a renewed motion by August 19.
This case is ongoing.

Plaintiffs, organizations that rely on IES research for education finance, policy, and higher education access and represented by Public Citizen Litigation Group, seek orders to restore contracts, vacate staff reductions, reverse data access terminations, and prevent further actions that hinder IES, and also request a temporary restraining order, preliminary injunction, and coverage of legal costs. evidence: In relevant part, EO 14248 seeks to make several changes to the rules governing elections. First, it directs the Election Assistance Committee (EAC) to alter the federal voter registration form prescribed by Congress (\"Federal Form\") to require documentary proof of United States citizenship. Second, it directs the EAC to change the Federal Form to require a state or local official to record on the form the type of documentary proof of U.S. citizenship that the voter provided. Third, it directs the EAC to take appropriate action to cease providing federal funds to states that do not comply with federal voting requirements, including the proof of citizenship requirement. Fourth, it directs the EAC to amend the Voluntary Voting System Guidelines (VVSG) 2.0 to prohibit the use of barcodes or \"quick response\" (QR) codes to encode votes and to require voting systems to provide a voter-verifiable paper record. Fifth, it directs the U.S. Attorney General to take all necessary action to enforce the federal statutes that establish a uniform election day for federal elections against states that include absentee or mail-in ballots received after election day in the final tabulation of votes. Finally, the EO directs the Secretary of Defense to update the Federal Post Card Application to require voters to provide documentary proof of citizenship and proof of eligibility to vote in the relevant state election.

On March 31, 2025, three nonprofits filed this lawsuit in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia. Represented by counsel from the State Democracy Defenders Fund and the Campaign Legal Center, they named the Executive Office of the President, the U.S. Election Assistance Commission and its director and commissioners, the U.S. Department of Justice, the U.S. Department of Defense, the Federal Voting Assistance Program, and their agency heads as Defendants.

On April 3, the case was consolidated with two other cases, Democratic National Committee et al. v. Trump et al., and League of Women Voters Education Fund et al. v. Trump et al. (linked below under Related Cases) that also challenged the EO.

The plaintiffs in all three cases alleged that the President exceeded his constitutional powers by purporting to impose federal election rules on states in violation of the Separation of Powers, the Constitution's Electors and Elections Clauses, the Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act, and the Administrative Procedure Act.

On April 24, 2025, she granted a preliminary injunction, barring operation of the Executive Order's Sections 2(a) and 2(d), which (a) order the Election Assistance Commission—a bipartisan, independent regulatory commission—to amend the standardized national voter registration form to require certain documentary proof of U.S. citizenship, and (b) order federal voter registration agencies to “assess” the citizenship of individuals who receive public assistance before providing them a voter registration form.

Since \"[o]ur Constitution entrusts Congress and the States—not the President—with the authority to regulate federal elections,\" the court found that the defendants' actions here were beyond their authority. \"Consistent with that allocation of power, Congress is currently debating legislation that would effect many of the changes the President purports to order,\" but the ability to unilaterally order such changes does not lie with the President. 2025 WL 1187730.

However, the court rejected (for now) the challenges to the other sections of the EO, stating with respect to some that the plaintiffs had failed to show that they were likely to succeed on the merits and that they had failed to demonstrate standing with regard to others. Therefore, the court declined to issue a preliminary injunction enjoining enforcement of Section 2(b), Section 7(a), and Section 7(b) of the EO.

On May 31, the defendants filed their answer to the complaint, arguing as affirmative defenses that the plaintiffs' claims were not ripe, that the plaintiffs lacked standing, and that the plaintiffs' claims were unreviewable under the APA.

The Republican National Committee (RNC) moved to intervene on June 3, asserting \"interests in ensuring 'that only qualified voters vote and that unqualified voters do not dilute the votes cast by lawful voters,' in promoting 'efficient election administration,' and in protecting 'their voters’ confidence in elections by ensuring the accuracy and integrity of election outcomes.'\" After the parties briefed the motion, the court granted the motion in part on June 12, allowing the RNC to intervene to defend Sections 2(a), 2(b), 2(d), 3(a), and 7(a) of the EO. The court set a schedule for the case on June 20.

On July 11, the plaintiffs filed a motion for partial summary judgment on Section 2(a) of the EO. Section 2(a) commands the EAC \"to amend the Federal Form to require that applicants provide one of the limited forms of citizenship documents the Executive Order specifies.\" Pointing to the court's earlier discussion of this section in its opinion granting a preliminary injunction, the plaintiffs argued that summary judgment on this portion of the EO was appropriate.
Discovery in the case is ongoing.

evidence: This case challenges the Trump Administration’s punitive measures against Columbia University for its asserted failure to address antisemitism on campus, including the cancellation of $400 million in federal research funding and demands for sweeping programmatic and structural changes.

On March 25, 2025, the American Association of University Professors (AAUP) and the American Federation of Teachers (AFT), two labor organizations for teachers and professors, filed this lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York against the U.S. Department of Justice, the U.S. Department of Education, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, the National Institutes of Health, the U.S. General Services Administration, and their corresponding agency heads.

Represented by Protect Democracy and private counsel, the plaintiffs sought a preliminary and permanent injunction requiring the restoration of funding and prohibiting further unlawful actions, declaratory relief, damages, and attorneys’ fees and costs.

Plaintiffs alleged that conditioning billions of dollars in congressionally authorized federal funding on Columbia University’s regulation of campus speech and expression violated the First Amendment by coercing Columbia to suppress student and faculty speech, particularly expression supportive of Palestinian rights.

The plaintiffs also raised a Fifth Amendment due process claim, asserting that the government failed to provide adequate notice or an opportunity to be heard before threatening severe financial penalties.

They maintained that the lack of any formal adjudication or evidentiary process deprived Columbia and its community of basic procedural protections, particularly given the vagueness of the government’s expectations and the absence of a clear standard for compliance.

In addition, the plaintiffs invoked the Tenth Amendment, arguing that the federal government exceeded its constitutional authority by attempting to control the internal operations of a private university, thereby encroaching on areas traditionally governed by state law and institutional autonomy.

Under the Spending Clause, the plaintiffs contended that the government’s threats were unlawful because the conditions imposed were not clearly stated, lacked a sufficient nexus to the purpose of the funding, and were unconstitutionally coercive.
They emphasized that the conditions were applied retroactively, were unrelated to the underlying federal programs and left the university with no real choice but to acquiesce.

The plaintiffs also asserted violations of the Administrative Procedure Act, arguing that the agencies involved lacked statutory authority for their actions and had bypassed necessary rulemaking procedures.
They described the agencies’ actions as arbitrary and capricious, driven by political pressure rather than formal findings of discrimination.
Finally, the plaintiffs raised a Separation of Powers concern, contending that the executive branch had unlawfully usurped powers reserved to Congress and the judiciary.

They argued that the administration’s proposed remedy—placing academic departments into federal receivership—had no legal basis and reflected an improper attempt to impose sanctions through executive fiat.
On April 3, 2025, plaintiffs filed a motion for a preliminary injunction.
On June 16, 2025, Judge Vyskocil denied this motion and dismissed the case without prejudice for lack of standing.
The court held that the plaintiff unions lacked standing because they could not demonstrate a concrete and particularized injury fairly traceable to the defendants’ alleged conduct.
The court emphasized that Columbia University itself was not a party to the lawsuit.
Without a direct plaintiff experiencing harm, the court concluded that the unions could not seek equitable relief such as reinstatement of funds or an injunction against the government.
Additionally, the court found that the unions failed to show a likelihood of success on the merits or irreparable harm necessary to justify preliminary relief.
As a result, the case was dismissed without prejudice and administratively closed.
That same day, the plaintiffs filed an appeal to the Second Circuit.
The appeal to the Second Circuit remains pending.
extracted.value: The case involves a lawsuit filed by the American Association of University Professors (AAUP) and the American Federation of Teachers (AFT) on March 25, 2025 in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York against the U.S. Department of Justice, the U.S. Department of Education, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, the National Institutes of Health, the U.S. General Services Administration, and their agency heads, alleging that the Trump Administration’s punitive measures—including cancellation of $400 million in federal research funding and demands for sweeping programmatic and structural changes—violated constitutional provisions (First, Fifth, Tenth, and Spending Clause) and the Administrative Procedure Act and Separation of Powers. The plaintiffs sought a preliminary and permanent injunction to restore funding, declaratory relief, damages, and attorneys’ fees, and claimed the government’s conditions were coercive, lacked due process, and exceeded federal authority. On April 3, 2025 a motion for a preliminary injunction was filed. On June 16, 2025 Judge Mary Kay Vyskocil denied the motion and dismissed the case without prejudice for lack of standing, finding the unions could not demonstrate a concrete injury or a likelihood of success on the merits. The plaintiffs appealed to the Second Circuit on the same day; the appeal remains pending.

evidence: This case involved a challenge to the Trump administration's effort to freeze federal grants for electric vehicle (EV) charging infrastructure.

On May 7, 2025, seventeen states and the District of Columbia sued the Department of Transportation and various sub-agencies and officials to stop the implementation of Executive Order 14,154, "Terminating the Green New Deal," which directed the Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) to suspend the National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (NEVI) Formula Program.

The states brought claims under the Administrative Procedure Act and the Constitution, alleging that the suspension of Formula grants for EV charging stations is unlawful and violates separation of powers.
The case was assigned to District Judge Tanya Lin.
On May 7, plaintiffs filed a motion for a preliminary injunction (PI).
On May 22, several public interest organizations, including the Sierra Club and the Natural Resources Defense Council, filed a motion to intervene as party plaintiffs.
Following a hearing on June 17, the court granted the motion for a PI as to 14 of the plaintiff states, finding a likelihood of success on the merits of their APA and separation of powers claims.
The court denied the motion in part, finding that the District of Columbia, Minnesota, and Vermont failed to demonstrate irreparable harm beyond the allegations set forth in the complaint.

Defendants were enjoined from suspending or revoking plaintiffs' previously approved State Electric Vehicle Infrastructure Deployment Plans – which are required annual submissions outlining how each state will use funding – and from withholding NEVI Formula Program funds.
The case is ongoing.

evidence: On May 5, 2025, nineteen states and the District of Columbia filed this lawsuit in the United States District Court for the District of Rhode Island against the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and numerous related federal agencies and their agency heads.
The states challenged layoffs that took place due to a March 27, 2025 directive that ordered a reduction in force of about 10,000 full-time employees.
The directive also ordered the restructuring of HHS, shrinking the previous twenty-eight divisions down to fifteen.
The layoffs took place on April 1.

Represented by their attorneys general, the states alleged that the dismantling of HHS left it incapable of performing its statutory functions in violation of the Separation of Powers, the Appropriations Clause, and the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).
The states also alleged that the defendants' actions were ultra vires in excess of their statutory authority.
On May 9, the plaintiffs moved for a preliminary injunction.
The case was assigned to District Judge Melissa R. DuBose, who held a hearing on the plaintiffs' motion for preliminary relief on May 22 and issued a preliminary injunction on July 1, 2025.

The court held that the states had standing to bring the lawsuit, that the claims were not subject to channeling pursuant to the Civil Service Reform Act, that the Tucker Act did not require the states to bring their claims in the Court of Federal Claims, that the March 27 directive constituted a final agency action subject to review under the APA, and that the states had demonstrated a likelihood of success on the merits of their claims that the challenged actions were arbitrary and capricious and contrary to law, had shown irreparable harm absent relief, and that the balance of equities and public interest weighed in their favor.

Accordingly, the court issued a preliminary injunction enjoining the defendants from 'taking any actions to implement or enforce the planned RIFs or sub-agency restructuring announced' in the directive.

On July 11, 2025, the defendants moved to clarify the preliminary injunction and also argued that the injunction was overbroad given the U.S. Supreme Court's decision in Casa Inc. v. Trump [../../../../case/45965/], which held that federal courts lacked the power to grant relief to parties outside of those involved in the case before them.
On July 17, 2025, the defendants also filed a motion to vacate the preliminary injunction, or in the alternative, to stay it pending appeal.

The defendants pointed to the decision of the U.S. Supreme Court in New York v. McMahon [../../../../case/46217/], which allowed the government to proceed with a reduction-in-force at the Department of Education while litigation over the RIF continued.

The defendants argued that '[b]ecause the facts and legal issues in [McMahon] are so similar to those presented here, the stays signal that a majority of the Supreme Court would likely reach the same conclusion if asked to consider this case.'

On July 18, 2025, the court denied all the defendants' motions except the motion to clarify, announcing that 'without any actual changes to governing case law or binding First Circuit or Supreme Court precedent, this Court declines the Defendants’ invitation to short circuit that process.'

On August 12, 2025, the court granted in part the defendants' motion to clarify the preliminary injunction and issued a revised injunction that named the specific sub-agencies and programs subject to the order.

The next day, the defendants filed an appeal in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit (USCA Case No. 25-1780) as well as an emergency motion in the appellate court to stay the injunction pending appeal.

The states alleged the dismantling violated the Separation of Powers, the Appropriations Clause, and the APA, and was ultra‑vires. The court held the states had standing, that the directive was a final agency action subject to APA review, and on July 1, 2025 issued a preliminary injunction preventing the implementation of the layoffs and restructuring. The defendants moved to clarify the injunction on July 11, 2025, and to vacate or stay it on July 17, 2025, citing Casa Inc. v. Trump and New York v. McMahon; the court denied these motions except for clarification, and on August 12, 2025 granted in part the clarification and revised the injunction. evidence:
On August 21, 2025, after a hearing, the court granting in part plaintiffs' motion for a preliminary injunction. 2025 WL 242325. First, it again found that it had jurisdiction over plaintiffs' claim, which neither challenged the fact nor the manner of detention or removal, nor sought to halt, suspend, or alter operation of any INA provision, nor otherwise challenged the defendants' authority to implement or enforce immigration laws (as would preclude jurisdiction under 8 U.S.C. 1252).  Next, the court held that the defendants had waived challenge to venue in the Southern District of Florida by litigating the case on the merits for a month before raising venue issues.  Rejecting the venue argument on the merits, it reasoned that the NEPA claim did not involve “real property” within the meaning of the applicable venue statute and therefore that venue was proper in the Southern District as the home of plaintiff's principal place of business, and not required to lie in the Middle District of Florida, where the facility is located.  Moreover, a substantial portion of events that gave rise to the lawsuit took place within the Southern District, and some of the environmental concerns relevant to the NEPA claim would also affect the Southern District.  Finally, the court found that the plaintiffs met the criteria for issuance of a preliminary injunction. As to a likelihood of success on the merits of plaintiffs' NEPA claims, the court noted that the defendants did not dispute the “major” environmental effects that would justify the need for an environmental impact statement or assessment.  Moreover, the decision to construct the detention camp without issuing an impact statement or conducting an assessment was a definitive position that caused actual, concrete injury to the plaintiffs' recreational and conservational interests, and therefore constituted a final agency action.  In addition, evidence the federal defendants requested that the facility be built and committed federal funding precluded them from dismissing involvement or responsibility under NEPA.  The environmental risks posed by the facility threatened irreparable harm to the plaintiffs, and the balance of equities and the public interest similarly favored granting the preliminary injunction.

Therefore, the court entered a preliminary injunction prohibiting the defendants and their officers, agents, employees, attorneys, and any person in active concert or participation with them from (1) installing any additional industrial-style lighting (so-called “Sunbelt” lighting); or doing any paving, filling, excavating, or fencing; or doing any other site expansion, including placing or erecting any additional buildings, tents, dormitories, or other residential or administrative facilities on the TNT site; and (2) bringing any additional persons onto the TNT site who were not already being detained at the site at the time the order went into effect. evidence:
On August 21, 2025, after a hearing, the court granting in part plaintiffs' motion for a preliminary injunction. 2025 WL 242325. First, it again found that it had jurisdiction over plaintiffs' claim, which neither challenged the fact nor the manner of detention or removal, nor sought to halt, suspend, or alter operation of any INA provision, nor otherwise challenged the defendants' authority to implement or enforce immigration laws (as would preclude jurisdiction under 8 U.S.C. 1252). Next, the court held that the defendants had waived challenge to venue in the Southern District of Florida by litigating the case on the merits for a month before raising venue issues. Rejecting the venue argument on the merits, it reasoned that the NEPA claim did not involve "real property" within the meaning of the applicable venue statute and therefore that venue was proper in the Southern District as the home of plaintiff's principal place of business, and not required to lie in the Middle District of Florida, where the facility is located. Moreover, a substantial portion of events that gave rise to the lawsuit took place within the Southern District, and some of the environmental concerns relevant to the NEPA claim would also affect the Southern District. Finally, the court found that the plaintiffs met the criteria for issuance of a preliminary injunction. As to a likelihood of success on the merits of plaintiffs' NEPA claims, the court noted that the defendants did not dispute the "major" environmental effects that would justify the need for an environmental impact statement or assessment. Moreover, the decision to construct the detention camp without issuing an impact statement or conducting an assessment was a definitive position that caused actual, concrete injury to the plaintiffs' recreational and conservational interests, and therefore constituted a final agency action. In addition, evidence the federal defendants requested that the facility be built and committed federal funding precluded them from dismissing involvement or responsibility under NEPA. The environmental risks posed by the facility threatened irreparable harm to the plaintiffs, and the balance of equities and the public interest similarly favored granting the preliminary injunction.

Therefore, the court entered a preliminary injunction prohibiting the defendants and their officers, agents, employees, attorneys, and any person in active concert or participation with them from (1) installing any additional industrial-style lighting (so-called “Sunbelt” lighting); or doing any paving, filling, excavating, or fencing; or doing any other site expansion, including placing or erecting any additional buildings, tents, dormitories, or other residential or administrative facilities on the TNT site; and (2) bringing any additional persons onto the TNT site who were not already being detained at the site at the time the order went into effect. The preliminary injunction did not prohibit modification or repairs to existing facilities that were made for the purpose of increasing safety or mitigating environmental or other risks at the site. It further ordered that after no more than sixty days, and once population attrition allowed for safe implementation, the defendants were to remove 1) the temporary fencing in order to allow tribe members access to the site consistent with the access they enjoyed before the facility was built; 2) the Sunbelt lighting fixtures and any additional lighting installed for the use of the property as a detention facility; and 3) all generators, gas, sewage, and other waste and waste receptacles that were installed for this project.

evidence: This case challenged the Trump administration’s 2025 suspension and termination of federal funding to Harvard University in response to alleged antisemitism on campus.

On April 11, 2025, the American Association of University Professors (AAUP), its Harvard Faculty Chapter (AAUP–Harvard), and the United Auto Workers (UAW) filed this lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts against the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ), Department of Education (ED), Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), and other federal agencies and officials.
The case was assigned to Judge Allison D. Burroughs.

Plaintiffs alleged that beginning in March 2025, the administration used Title VI enforcement powers and federal grant authority to compel Harvard to restructure its internal operations in ways that violated academic freedom and chilled speech on matters related to Israel and antisemitism.
On March 31, the DOJ announced a review of Harvard’s civil rights compliance.
In letters dated April 3 and April 11, multiple agencies demanded that Harvard implement sweeping governance and curricular changes as conditions for continued funding.
When Harvard refused, agencies began canceling grants and contracts, ultimately affecting over $9 billion in research funding.
Plaintiffs claimed these actions violated the First and Fifth Amendments, the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), and Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
Plaintiffs moved for a temporary restraining order (TRO) on April 11, and then for summary judgment on June 2.

They sought a declaration that the agencies’ actions were unlawful and a permanent injunction prohibiting any further funding terminations or conditions that infringed constitutional rights or bypassed statutory procedures.

The government opposed the motions and cross-moved for summary judgment, arguing that plaintiffs lacked standing and that the agency actions were lawful exercises of grant authority under 2 C.F.R. § 200.340(a)(4).
The government further asserted that no final agency action had occurred and that plaintiffs could not enforce Harvard’s contractual rights.
Plaintiffs withdrew their TRO motion on April 15, citing changed circumstances and reserving the right to seek other preliminary relief.

Several amici filed briefs in support of plaintiffs. Public Citizen argued that the administration’s actions targeted protected speech and undermined university autonomy. A Jewish Voice for Peace challenged the administration’s definition of antisemitism, warning that it blurred religious and political categories in violation of the Establishment Clause. Other briefs emphasized the broader impact on research, student expression, and economic innovation.
A hearing on the cross-motions for summary judgment was scheduled for July 21, 2025. As of mid-July 2025, no ruling had issued.

A related case—President and Fellows of Harvard College v. U.S. Department of Justice [../../../../case/46442/]—was filed separately by Harvard University itself. The case remains ongoing as of July 16, 2025.

evidence: This case challenged the freezing of federal grant funds meant for green infrastructure projects. Plaintiffs, the Climate United Fund, a non profit financial institution, filed a lawsuit in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia. The plaintiffs named Citibank, N.A., the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), and the EPA Administrator as the defendants.

The dispute stemmed from the National Clean Investment Fund (NCIF), a program under the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund (GGRF), which Congress established through the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022. Climate United was selected as a grantee in April 2024, receiving $6.97 billion in funding to support clean energy projects across the United States, particularly in low-income, rural, and tribal communities. Under the terms of the grant, Climate United’s funds were held at Citibank, which served as a financial agent under an Account Control Agreement (ACA) executed with the EPA.

Problems began in early 2025 after the EPA administrator publicly expressed opposition to the GGRF, calling it 'criminal' and vowing to recover the funds. On February 18, 2025, Climate United submitted a routine request to withdraw funds from its Citibank account. However, Citibank refused to process the transaction, citing the need for further guidance from the EPA.

In its complaint filed on March 8, 2025 (and subsequent amended complaint on March 17), Climate United claimed that Citibank breached its contractual obligations under the ACA by refusing to disburse funds.

evidence: This lawsuit challenged three executive orders issued by President Donald Trump in January 2025, which significantly altered federal policies on diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility (DEIA) programs and transgender rights.

On February 19, 2025, the National Urban League (NUL), the National Fair Housing Alliance (NFHA), and the AIDS Foundation of Chicago (AFC) filed this lawsuit in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia.

They named as defendants: President Trump, the Office of Management and Budget, the Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs, the U.S. Department of Labor, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, U.S. Department of Commerce, U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, U.S. Department of Agriculture, the National Institutes of Health, the Health Resources and Services Administration, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the Administration for Community Living, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, the U.S. Department of Justice, and their corresponding agency heads.
The plaintiffs sought injunctive and declaratory relief, arguing these executive orders violated the First and Fifth Amendments of the U.S. Constitution and the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).

First, Executive Order 14151, titled “Ending Radical and Wasteful DEI Programs and Preferencing” (Jan. 20, 2025), which terminated all federal DEIA programs, positions, grants, and contracts. Second, Executive Order 14168 titled “Defending Women From Gender Ideology Extremism and Restoring Biological Truth to the Federal Government” (Jan. 20, 2025), which eliminated federal recognition of transgender identities and barred agencies from funding “gender ideology.” Third, Executive Order 14173 titled “Ending Illegal Discrimination and Restoring Merit-Based Opportunity” (Jan. 21, 2025), which banned federal contractors and grantees from using DEIA programs and imposed penalties for noncompliance.

The plaintiffs argued these executive orders were in violation of the First Amendment for (1) chilling the plaintiffs’ speech, (2) imposing an unconstitutional restriction on speech, (3) content and viewpoint discrimination, and (4) impermissibly conditioning funding on the relinquishment of plaintiffs’ free speech rights. They also argued the orders violated the Fifth Amendment for being impermissibly vague, thereby allowing for discriminatory and arbitrary enforcement, and denying people adequate notice as to what speech and activities were prohibited. They also argued the orders violated Equal Protection under the Fifth Amendment for discrimination on the basis of race, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, and transgender status. Finally, they argued the orders violated the Administrative Procedure Act for being arbitrary, capricious, and exceeding executive authority.

Plaintiffs requested a declaration that the executive orders were unlawful, unconstitutional, and invalid. They also sought a permanent injunction against the enforcement and implementation of the orders, as well as requiring the defendants to rescind all agency-wide directives implementing the orders.

The plaintiffs filed a motion for a preliminary injunction on February 28, requesting that defendants be prohibited from "enforcing and implementing key provisions of Executive Order Nos. 14151, 14168, and 141734."

The defendants' opposition, filed March 12, argued that (1) the plaintiffs' Fifth Amendment claim failed on the merits because the void-for-vagueness doctrine did not apply where "the President direct[ed] his own subordinates with respect to policy and enforcement priorities;" and (2) the First Amendment claim failed because the plaintiffs did not properly establish that the orders "prohibit[ed] a substantial amount of protected speech relative to [their] plainly legitimate sweep," so as to be facial unconstitutional.

After a hearing on March 19, the court rejected the preliminary injunction on May 2, 2025, writing: For half the challenged provisions, Plaintiffs fail to establish a prerequisite to success on the merits: standing. Presidential directives to subordinates that inflict no concrete harm on private parties—or at least not on these parties—do not present a justiciable case or controversy. And for the remaining provisions, Plaintiffs’ constitutional claims falter for various reasons. Two throughlines explain most of them. The government need not subsidize the exercise of constitutional rights to avoid infringing them, and the Constitution does not provide a right to violate federal antidiscrimination law. And those pressure points are even harder to overcome for Plaintiffs, who bring facial rather than as-applied challenges.
On May 20, the parties filed a joint motion proposing a schedule for the case going forward. The first deadline was on June 27, when the plaintiffs filed their first amended complaint.

The amended complaint removed a plaintiff, the National Fair Housing Alliance, and any related factual and legal allegations. The amended complaint added additional details regarding more examples of harm and chilling effects resulting from the defendants' actions. These allegations were intended to support the plaintiffs' First Amendment claims. Finally, the amended complaint removed the plaintiffs' claims under the APA, leaving only their First and Fifth Amendment claims.
The court ordered the defendants to file a response to the amended complaint by August 8.
extracted.value: The case involves a lawsuit filed on February 19, 2025 by the National Urban League, the National Fair Housing Alliance, and the AIDS Foundation of Chicago, challenging three executive orders issued by President Donald Trump on January 20–21, 2025 that terminated federal DEIA programs, eliminated recognition of transgender identities, and banned DEIA programs for contractors. The plaintiffs alleged violations of the First and Fifth Amendments and sought injunctive and declaratory relief. The defendants include President Trump and numerous federal agencies. The court denied a preliminary injunction and later the plaintiffs amended the complaint, removing the National Fair Housing Alliance and APA claims, and adding more examples of harm. The case remains pending.

evidence: On February 11, 2025, the Global Health Council and several non-profit organizations filed this lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia against President Donald J. Trump, the U.S. State Department of State, the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), and USAID.

Represented by private counsel, Plaintiffs alleged that a January 20, 2025 Executive Order (EO) calling for the suspension of foreign aid funding and subsequent implementation guidance from the State Department, USAID, and OMB terminating existing foreign aid obligations violated the Administrative Procedure Act and Separation of Powers.

The next day, the Court issued a TRO prohibiting the State Department, USAID, and OMB from pausing disbursement of congressionally-appropriated foreign assistance funds on contracts that were in place as of January 19, 2025.

The court issued a PI on March 10 prohibiting Defendants from enforcing the State Department guidance regarding implementation of the EO, or giving effect to any actions taken to restrain foreign assistance between January 20 and February 13, 2025.
The Court ordered Defendants to submit a status report detailing their compliance with the order by February 18, 2025.

This case challenged the Trump Administration's authority to suspend nearly all congressionally-appropriated foreign assistance funding and dismantle the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID).

evidence: On January 8, 2013, Judge Scheindlin ruled for the plaintiffs, finding that they had demonstrated the likelihood that they would prevail on the merits, and proved the city's deliberate indifference toward a widespread practice of unconstitutional trespass stops by the NYPD outside TAP buildings in the Bronx. Judge Scheindlin summarized that her conclusion was based on five categories of evidence: (1) the testimony of a Bronx Assistant District Attorney that the NYPD frequently made trespass stops outside TAP buildings in the Bronx for no reason other than that the officer had seen someone enter and exit or exit the building; (2) a sample of "decline to prosecute" forms prepared by the Bronx District Attorneys' Office, which revealed the alarming frequency of unlawful trespass stops in the vicinity of TAP buildings in the Bronx; (3) the testimony of eight plaintiffs and a non-party witness, who described remarkably similar encounters with the police when stopped in the vicinity of TAP buildings in the Bronx; (4) the analysis by Dr. Jeffrey Fagan, plaintiffs' expert, of an NYPD database of recorded stops, which provided further evidence of the frequency of apparently unlawful trespass stops outside TAP buildings in the Bronx; and (5) NYPD training materials that misstated the minimal constitutional standards for making stops. The Court issued a preliminary injunction, ordering the NYPD to immediately cease performing trespass stops (in which a reasonable person would not feel free to terminate the encounter) outside TAP buildings in the Bronx without reasonable suspicion of trespass. In addition, Judge Scheindlin set out proposed relief, and consolidated a hearing on it with the already-scheduled remedial hearing in the related Floyd litigation.
extracted.value: Ligon v. City of New York consolidated its preliminary injunction hearing with the remedial hearing in Floyd v. City of New York.
